Sleep

How many hours of sleep do you need?

Adults need between seven and nine hours, but regularity matters as much as quantity.

"Five hours is enough for me" is something you hear often. Some people say it with pride, as if sleeping little were a virtue. How much do we really need?

The recommendations

In 2015, a panel of experts from the US National Sleep Foundation reviewed hundreds of studies and proposed recommended hours by age:

  • Adults aged 18 to 64: between 7 and 9 hours.
  • Over 65s: between 7 and 8 hours.
  • Teenagers aged 14 to 17: between 8 and 10 hours.
  • Children aged 6 to 13: between 9 and 11 hours.

There is individual variation, but people who genuinely function well on less than six hours are very few. Most who think it is enough have got used to being tired and no longer notice it, even though their attention and memory suffer on tests.

Why it matters

During sleep the brain consolidates what it has learned, regulates emotions and does cleaning work. Chronic short sleep is linked to worse mood, more irritability, more accidents and higher risk of health problems such as high blood pressure or diabetes.

Larks and owls

We do not all have the same internal clock. Some people, "larks", become alert early and get sleepy early; others, "owls", perform better in the evening and fall asleep late. This is the chronotype, which depends partly on genes and changes with age: teenagers are more nocturnal. Till Roenneberg called the gap between the schedule set by our biological clock and the one imposed by work or school social jet lag, and it mostly affects owls.

Catching up at the weekend

Sleeping longer at the weekend relieves tiredness, but it does not fix everything. In an experiment by Christopher Depner, people who slept little during the week and caught up at the weekend kept alterations in blood sugar metabolism similar to those of people who slept little every day. The healthiest option is a regular schedule, including at weekends.

What usually helps

  • Regular hours, at weekends too: your internal clock appreciates consistency.
  • Natural light in the morning and little bright light at night.
  • Bed is for sleeping: if you have been lying awake a long time, get up and go back when you feel sleepy.
  • Watch caffeine from mid-afternoon onwards and alcohol, which fragments sleep.
If you sleep badly almost every night for months, see your doctor. Chronic insomnia has effective drug-free treatments.

References

  1. Hirshkowitz, M. et al. (2015). National Sleep Foundation's sleep time duration recommendations: methodology and results summary. Sleep Health, 1(1), 40–43.
  2. Van Dongen, H. P. A. et al. (2003). The cumulative cost of additional wakefulness. Sleep, 26(2), 117–126.
  3. Wittmann, M., Dinich, J., Merrow, M. y Roenneberg, T. (2006). Social jetlag: misalignment of biological and social time. Chronobiology International, 23(1–2), 497–509.
  4. Depner, C. M. et al. (2019). Ad libitum weekend recovery sleep fails to prevent metabolic dysregulation during a repeating pattern of insufficient sleep and weekend recovery sleep. Current Biology, 29(6), 957–967.
